claim: CIC is frequently altered in human cancer and functionally suppresses tumor growth and metastasis
source: CIC is frequently altered in human cancer, where it functionally suppresses tumor growth and metastasis (Ahmad et al., 2019; Bettegowda et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2015; Dissanayake et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2018; Okimoto et al., 2017; Seim et al., 2017; Yoshiya et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: CIC is commonly altered through genomic loss in approximately 10% of prostate cancer patients
source: Notably, in PCa, CIC is commonly altered through genomic loss (homozygous and heterozygous deletion) in ~10% of PCa patients (Abida et al., 2019; Grasso et al., 2012; Hieronymus et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2017; Robinson et al., 2015; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple prostate cancer genomic studies

claim: ERF is a transcriptional repressor that binds ETS DNA motifs
source: Since ERF is a transcriptional repressor that binds ETS DNA motifs (Bose et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Bose et al., 2017)

claim: CIC and ERF co-deletions occur with high frequency (p<0.001) in prostate cancer
source: identified a high cooccurrence rate (p<0.001, two-sided Fisher's exact test [FET]) for CIC (10%) and ERF (12%) homozygous and heterozygous deletions (Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of 15 PCa datasets shown in Figure 1C

claim: CIC-ERF co-deletion is present at increased frequency in prostate cancer with higher Gleason scores and later tumor stages
source: we observed that the CIC-ERF co-deletion was present at an increased frequency in PCa with higher Gleason scores and later tumor stages when compared to CIC-ERF replete tumors (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of clinically annotated specimens shown in Figure 1D

claim: CIC and ERF alterations are enriched in metastatic castrate resistant prostate cancer compared to primary prostate cancer
source: This analysis revealed enrichment of CIC and ERF alterations including the CIC-ERF co-deletion in mCRPC samples (Figure 1E, Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of primary vs. metastatic PCa datasets shown in Figure 1E

claim: CIC-ERF co-deleted tumors cluster as a distinct molecular subgroup separate from ERG, ETV1, ETV4, SPOP, and FOXA1 altered prostate cancers
source: Importantly, CIC-ERF co-deleted tumors clustered as a subgroup when compared to the more well-characterized molecular subsets including ERG, ETV1, ETV4, SPOP, and FOXA1 altered PCas, suggesting a distinct molecular subtype of PCa (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 1F

claim: Patients with CIC-ERF co-deletion have significantly worse disease-free survival (p=0.001) and progression-free survival (p=0.01)
source: we performed a survival analysis using the aforementioned PCa datasets and observed significantly worse outcomes in patients who harbored the CIC-ERF co-deletion (p=0.001, disease-free survival [DFS] [ERF-CIC co-deletion 25 events/90 total; no ERF-CIC co-deletion 153 events/910 total] and p=0.01, progression-free survival [PFS] [ERF-CIC co-deletion 16 events/52 total; no ERF-CIC co-deletion 77 events/442 total]; Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 1G with specific p-values and event counts

claim: Genetic inactivation of both CIC and ERF increases colony formation compared to single gene loss in PNT2 cells
source: Compared to single gene loss of CIC or ERF, genetic inactivation of both CIC and ERF increased colony formation (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B

claim: CIC-ERF co-deletion enhances spheroid formation in PNT2 cells
source: CIC-ERF co-deletion also enhanced malignant phenotypes including cellular viability, invasiveness, and migratory capacity in PNT2 (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C-D and 2E-G

claim: Genetic silencing of both CIC and ERF increases the frequency of subcutaneous tumor xenograft formation in SCID mice
source: Additionally, genetic silencing of both CIC and ERF increased the frequency of subcutaneous tumor xenograft formation in severe-combined immunodeficient (SCID) mice compared to control (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figure 2H

claim: DU-145 cells harbor a loss-of-function ERF mutation (ERFA132S) and express functional wild-type CIC
source: DU-145 cells harbor a loss-of-function ERF mutation (ERFA132S) (Huang et al., 2017) and express functional WT CIC, (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation and validation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: PC-3 cells are deficient in CIC (homozygous deletion) and retain functional ERF
source: By comparison, PC-3 cells are deficient in CIC (homozygous deletion) and retain functional ERF (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Cerami et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013; Seim et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and validation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Genetic reconstitution of ERF into ERF-deficient DU-145 cells decreases colony formation in both CIC proficient and CIC knockout conditions
source: Specifically, genetic reconstitution of ERF into ERF-deficient DU-145 cells decreased colony formation in both CIC proficient (parental cells) and CIC knockout (KO) conditions (Figure 3A–B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B

claim: ERF expression in CIC KO DU-145 cells rescues the CIC-mediated effects on viability and migration/invasion
source: Importantly, we observed that ERF expression in CIC KO DU-145 cells rescued the CIC-mediated effects on viability and migration/invasion (Figure 3C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D

claim: CIC knockout increases tumor growth rate in DU-145 xenografts in vivo
source: Consistent with our in vitro data, CIC KO increased the tumor growth rate in vivo and genetic reconstitution of WT ERF partially suppressed tumor growth compared to DU-145 CIC KO cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Genetic reconstitution of ERF into CIC proficient DU-145 cells suppresses tumor growth rate in vivo
source: Moreover, genetic reconstitution of ERF into CIC proficient DU-145 cells suppressed the tumor growth rate in vivo (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figure 3E

claim: ERF overexpression or CIC reconstitution decreases PC-3 colony formation, with combinatorial ERF OE and CIC rescue having the most significant reduction
source: We first noted that ERF overexpression (OE) or reconstitution of CIC alone decreased PC-3 colony formation, with combinatorial ERF OE and CIC rescue having the most significant reduction compared to parental PC-3 cells (Figure 3F–G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F-G

claim: ERF overexpression in CIC deficient PC-3 tumor xenografts decreases tumor growth compared to PC-3 parental and PC-3 cells expressing wild-type CIC
source: Interestingly, OE of ERF in mice bearing CIC deficient PC-3 tumor xenografts decreased tumor growth compared to PC-3 parental and PC-3 cells expressing WT CIC (genetic rescue of CIC; Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figure 3J

claim: ChIP-Seq analysis identified 178 high-confidence CIC peaks that mapped to 130 annotated genes including ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5
source: This analysis identified 178 high-confidence (False-discovery rate (FDR) ≤0.05) CIC peaks that mapped to 130 annotated genes including known targets, ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq experimental data with specific FDR threshold

claim: CIC peaks are localized to promoters (38.6%), UTRs (1.14%), introns (19.9%), and distal intergenic regions (38.64%)
source: Globally, CIC peaks were localized to distinct genomic regions including promoters (38.6%), untranslated regions (UTRs) (1.14%), introns (19.9%), and distal intergenic regions (38.64%).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq analysis data with specific percentages

claim: ERF peaks are distributed to promoters (32.8%), UTRs (1.2%), introns (29.2%), and distal intergenic regions (33.8%)
source: Interestingly, the distribution of ERF peaks was similar to CIC, with 32.8% in promoters, 1.2% in UTRs, 29.2% intronic, and 33.8% in distal intergenic regions (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq analysis data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Comparative ChIP-Seq analysis identified 91 shared CIC and ERF target genes
source: Next, through a comparative ChIP-Seq analysis (Figure 4B), we identified 91 shared CIC and ERF target genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative ChIP-Seq analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: PEA3 family transcription factors (ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5) are the most highly enriched family among shared CIC and ERF target genes
source: Among these putative CIC and ERF targets, the PEA3 (ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5) TFs (known oncogenic drivers in PCa; Baena et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2012) were found to be the most highly enriched family.
evidence: The claim is supported by Functional Clustering Analysis using DAVID bioinformatics database

claim: CIC knockout and/or combinatorial CIC and ERF loss in PNT2 cells increases ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5 levels compared to control
source: As expected, CIC KO and/or combinatorial CIC and ERF loss in PNT2 cells (ERF and CIC WT) consistently increased ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5 levels compared to control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-F

claim: Genetic silencing of ERF consistently increases ETV1 mRNA expression, but not ETV4 or ETV5
source: In contrast, genetic silencing of ERF consistently increased ETV1 mRNA expression, but not ETV4 or ETV5 (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-J).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-J

claim: CIC and ERF do not physically interact based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments
source: In order to test a potential proteomic interaction between CIC and ERF, we performed co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) experiments but did not observe binding when either ERF or CIC was pulled down in HEK293T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K-L).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K-L

claim: CIC and ERF independently bind to the proximal ETV1 regulatory element
source: we first localized CIC (TGAATGGA) and ERF (GGAA) DNA binding motifs within the proximal upstream regulatory element of ETV1 and independently confirmed CIC and ERF occupancy of the ETV1 promoter through ChIP-PCR (Figure 4D–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, P).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 4D-G

claim: ERF reconstitution in ERF deficient DU-145 cells decreases ETV1 expression in both CIC proficient and CIC deficient settings
source: To extend these findings into the context of PCa, we reconstituted ERF in ERF deficient DU-145 cells and this consistently decreased ETV1 expression (not ETV4 or ETV5) in both CIC proficient and CIC deficient settings (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1Q-T).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4H

claim: ERF knockdown in CIC deficient PC-3 cells increases ETV1 mRNA expression
source: Moreover, ERF Knockdown (KD) or ERF OE in CIC deficient PC-3 cells increased and decreased ETV1 mRNA expression, respectively (Figure 4I–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4I-J

claim: ERF expression decreases luciferase activity in ETV1 promoter assays in 293T cells
source: To this end, we engineered a ETV1 luciferase based promoter assays and observed a decrease in luciferase activity following ERF expression in 293T cells (Figure 4K).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase promoter assay data shown in Figure 4K

claim: Dual CIC and ERF deficiency is significantly associated with the ETV1-regulated gene set (IC=0.619, p=0.0009)
source: We found that CIC and ERF loss were significantly associated with the ETV1-regulated gene set (Information coefficient (IC)=0.619, p=0.0009)
evidence: The claim is supported by ssGSEA analysis with specific IC and p-value

claim: Dual CIC and ERF deficiency is anti-correlated with the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion signature gene set (IC=-0.45, p=0.0009)
source: but was anti-correlated with the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion signature gene set (Setlur et al., 2008; Figure 4L, IC = –0.45, p=0.0009).
evidence: The claim is supported by ssGSEA analysis shown in Figure 4L with specific IC and p-value

claim: Silencing CIC in ERF-deficient DU-145 cells mildly enhances sensitivity to ETV1 inhibitor BRD32048
source: we unexpectedly observed that silencing CIC in DU-145 cells mildly enhanced sensitivity to BRD32048 (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by drug sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Viability of DU-145 CIC KO cells is decreased upon genetic ETV1 inhibition
source: Consistent with our pharmacologic studies, the viability of DU-145 CIC KO cells was decreased upon genetic ETV1 inhibition (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Pharmacologic and genetic ETV1 inhibition decreases invasiveness of CIC deficient DU-145 cells
source: Similarly, pharmacologic and genetic ETV1 inhibition decreased invasiveness of CIC deficient DU-145 cells (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 5C-D

claim: ETV1 inhibition decreases viability and invasiveness in PNT2 cells with dual ERF and CIC suppression
source: To expand these findings, we also consistently observed a decrease in viability and invasiveness upon ETV1 inhibition (BRD32048) in PNT2 cells with dual ERF and CIC suppression and in PC-3 cells with ERF KD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-J

claim: Activation of ETS transcription factors (ERG, ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5) is present in approximately 60% of prostate cancer
source: Activation of ETS transcription factors (TFs), ERG, ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5, are present in approximately 60% of PCa, underscoring their importance in prostate oncogenesis (Nelson et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Nelson et al., 2003)

claim: ETS transcription factors are most commonly activated through gene rearrangements that fuse TMPRSS2 to ERG, ETV1, ETV4, or ETV5
source: In human PCa, ETS TFs are most commonly activated through gene rearrangements that fuse the androgen responsive gene, TMPRSS2, to either ERG, ETV1, ETV4, or ETV5 (Sizemore et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Sizemore et al., 2017)

claim: Increased expression of wildtype ETS factors confers aggressive malignant phenotypes and associates with poor clinical outcomes in fusion negative prostate cancer patients
source: Beyond ETS TF fusions, little is known about the underlying molecular mechanisms that lead to increased expression of wildtype (WT) ETS factors, which confer aggressive malignant phenotypes and associate with poor clinical outcomes in fusion negative PCa patients (Baena et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Baena et al., 2013)

claim: CIC is a High-mobility group (HMG) box transcription factor
source: Capicua (CIC) is a High-mobility group (HMG) box TF that silences ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5 through direct target gene repression (Kim et al., 2021; Simón-Carrasco et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by citations

claim: Inactivation of CIC de-represses ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5 transcription to promote tumor progression
source: inactivation of CIC de-represses ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5 transcription to promote tumor progression (Bettegowda et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2018; Okimoto et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: CIC and ERF are separated by approximately 15 kb (long isoform) and 30 kb (short isoform) in the genome
source: long and short isoforms of CIC are separated from ERF by approximately 15 and 30 kb, respectively
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text based on genomic location data

claim: Concurrent loss of CIC and ERF most commonly occurs through focal genomic deletions at chromosome 19q13.2
source: Concurrent CIC and ERF loss commonly occur through focal genomic deletions at chromosome 19q13.2.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by genomic analysis data

claim: CIC and ERF co-bind the proximal regulatory element and mutually repress ETV1
source: Mechanistically, CIC and ERF co-bind the proximal regulatory element and mutually repress the ETS transcription factor, ETV1.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-Seq and functional data throughout the manuscript

claim: Targeting ETV1 in CIC and ERF-deficient prostate cancer limits tumor growth
source: Targeting ETV1 in CIC and ERF-deficient prostate cancer limits tumor growth.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5

claim: CIC binds to a highly conserved DNA-binding motif (T[G/C]AAT[G/A]AA)
source: CIC silences target genes through direct binding of a highly conserved DNA-binding motif (T[G/C]AAT[G/A]AA; Figure 1A; Ajuria et al., 2011; Futran et al., 2015; Jiménez et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A

claim: ERF binds and competes for ETS TF-binding sites (GGAA-motifs)
source: ERF binds and competes for ETS TF-binding sites (GGAA-motifs) and is frequently altered in human PCa, predominantly through focal deletions (Bose et al., 2017; Hou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research

claim: CIC and ERF are co-deleted in approximately 10% and 12% of prostate cancer patients, respectively
source: we first queried 15 PCa datasets curated on cBioPortal (Cerami et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013) and identified a high cooccurrence rate (p<0.001, two-sided Fisher's exact test [FET]) for CIC (10%) and ERF (12%) homozygous and heterozygous deletions
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of 15 PCa datasets with specific percentages

claim: CIC-ERF co-deleted tumors do not frequently co-occur with other known oncogenic events (ERG, ETV1, ETV4, SPOP, and FOXA1)
source: CIC-ERF co-deleted prostate tumors (red box) do not frequently co-occur with other known oncogenic events.
evidence: The claim is shown in Figure 1F caption and supported by oncoprint analysis

claim: Combination of CIC and ERF loss augments the transformation of PNT2 cells
source: Thus, our findings demonstrate that the combination of CIC and ERF loss augments the transformation of PNT2 and promotes malignant phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple in vitro and in vivo experiments shown in Figure 2

claim: CIC loss increases ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5 levels in PNT2 cells
source: As expected, CIC KO and/or combinatorial CIC and ERF loss in PNT2 cells (ERF and CIC WT) consistently increased ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5 levels compared to control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the phrase 'as expected' and supported by qRT-PCR data

claim: ETV1 is a novel ERF target gene
source: Therefore, we reveal ETV1 as a novel ERF target gene.
evidence: The claim is stated explicitly and supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including ChIP-PCR and luciferase assays

claim: ERF can suppress ETV1 expression through direct transcriptional silencing of the ETV1 promoter
source: These genetic tools further validate that ERF can suppress ETV1 expression through direct transcriptional silencing of the ETV1 promoter and identifies ETV1 as an ERF target.
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase promoter assay and ChIP-PCR data

claim: Dual suppression of CIC and ERF increases ETV1-mediated transcriptional programs in prostate cancer
source: These findings led us to hypothesize that the dual suppression of CIC and ERF may increase ETV1-mediated transcriptional programs in PCa.
evidence: The claim is stated as a hypothesis supported by ssGSEA analysis and functional data

claim: Loss of CIC in ERF-deficient prostate cancer cells can potentially modulate the sensitivity to ETV1-directed therapies
source: These findings indicate that loss of CIC in ERF deficient PCa cells can potentially modulate the sensitivity to ETV1-directed therapies.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug sensitivity and genetic inhibition experiments shown in Figure 5

claim: CIC and ERF cooperate to silence ETV1 transcriptional programs, limiting ETV1-mediated prostate cancer progression
source: Collectively, our data indicate that CIC and ERF may cooperate to silence ETV1 transcriptional programs, limiting ETV1-mediated PCa progression.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence throughout the manuscript

claim: The predominant mode of ETS activation in prostate cancer is through chromosomal rearrangements that fuse TMPRSS2 to ETS family members
source: The predominant mode of ETS activation in PCa is through chromosomal rearrangements that fuse ERG, ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5 to the androgen-regulated TMPRSS2 gene, leading to fusion oncoproteins that drive oncogenesis (Clark and Cooper, 2009; Feng et al., 2014; Helgeson et al., 2008; Tomlins et al., 2006; Tomlins et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5 are upregulated in a fusion-independent manner and are associated with poor clinical outcomes in prostate cancer patients
source: Interestingly, recent data indicate that ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5 are upregulated in a fusion-independent manner and are associated with poor clinical outcomes in PCa patients (Baena et al., 2013; Hermans et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research

claim: CIC-ERF co-deletion represents a new molecular subclass of prostate cancer
source: Our study focused on understanding the molecular mechanisms that drive fusion-independent upregulation of ETS family members and we reveal a new molecular subclass of PCa defined by a co-deletion of two TFs, CIC and ERF.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by clustering analysis and clinical data

claim: CIC and ERF are co-deleted in a subset of stomach adenocarcinoma
source: Beyond PCa, we and others have observed that CIC and ERF are co-deleted in a subset of stomach adenocarcinoma (LeBlanc et al., 2017; Okimoto et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research

claim: Combined CIC and ERF loss is not entirely specific for prostate cancer
source: Thus, combined CIC and ERF loss are not entirely specific for PCa.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion based on observations in stomach adenocarcinoma

claim: Prostate cancer is highly dependent on PEA3 transcriptional dysregulation to enhance tumor progression
source: We speculate that since prostate (Baena et al., 2013) and potentially stomach adenocarcinoma (Keld et al., 2011) are highly dependent on PEA3 transcriptional dysregulation to enhance tumor progression
evidence: The claim is stated as speculation supported by citations

claim: Dual loss of CIC and ERF may represent an alternative mode to de-repress ETS mediated transcriptional programs in prostate and stomach adenocarcinoma
source: the dual loss of CIC and ERF may, in part, represent an alternative mode to de-repress ETS mediated transcriptional programs in these cancer subsets.
evidence: The claim is stated as speculation based on observations in multiple cancer types

claim: Patients with CIC-ERF deficient prostate cancer may potentially benefit from ETV1 directed therapies
source: Our findings indicate that patients with CIC-ERF deficient PCa may have a survival dependence on ETV1 and that these patients may potentially benefit from ETV1 directed therapies.
evidence: The claim is stated as a potential therapeutic implication based on experimental data

claim: There is no statistically significant difference in ETV1 transcript levels in CIC-ERF co-deleted tumors compared to CIC-ERF replete tumors in the TCGA-PRAD dataset
source: A limitation of this targeted approach in PCa patients is that we did not find a statistically significant difference in ETV1 transcript levels in CIC-ERF co-deleted tumors compared to CIC-ERF replete tumors in the TCGA-PRAD (n=455) dataset.
evidence: The claim is stated as a limitation based on analysis of TCGA-PRAD dataset

claim: ETV1 is commonly upregulated in human prostate cancers through mechanisms beyond CIC-ERF loss
source: One potential explanation is that ETV1 is commonly upregulated in human PCas through mechanisms beyond CIC-ERF loss.
evidence: The claim is stated as a potential explanation for the lack of differential ETV1 expression
